title: Social epidemiology of bedtime screen use behaviors and sleep outcomes in early adolescence
authors: Nagata JM, Shim J, Ramappa S, Deshpande I, Low P, Kiss O, Ganson KT, Testa A, He J, Baker FC
journal: Sleep Health: Journal of the National Sleep Foundation

primary_models.name: Multivariable logistic regression of binary sleep disturbance (SDSC >= 39) on bedtime phone/SM behaviors, adjusted for sociodemographics and site, ACS-weighted
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 4, Sleep disturbance scale columns (p. 568); methods p. 564; results p. 565; sex-stratified version in Table 5 (see M4)
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional analysis of the ABCD Year 3 follow-up (2019-2021). Bedtime screen behaviors and sleep disturbance both measured at Year 3. One observation per participant; no repeated measures.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Year 3 follow-up; data release not stated. Of 11,875 enrolled, participants missing bedtime screen use responses were excluded, leaving N = 10,305 (complete case analysis; comparison of included vs excluded in online Appendix A). Mean age 12.93 (SD 0.65) years; 48.4% female, 51.6% male; 54.9% White, 19.6% Latino/Hispanic, 15.4% Black, 5.5% Asian, 3.1% Native American, 1.4% Other (weighted, Table 1). 84.3% assessed during the COVID-19 pandemic.
primary_models.iv: Single items from an 11-item bedtime screen use questionnaire completed by the adolescent, asking on how many nights in the past week they engaged in each activity while already in bed before going to sleep, rated on a five-point Likert scale from 1 (never) to 5 (every night); each item entered on that 1-5 scale. Qualifying items: 'Talk on the phone or text' (Table 2 distribution: 0 nights 54.4%, 1-2 nights 23.4%, 3-4 nights 12.5%, 5-7 nights 9.7%); 'Spend time online on social media (e.g., Facebook)' (56.1%, 20.2%, 12.6%, 11.2%); and 'In the past week, how often have you had phone calls, text messages, or emails that wake you after trying to go to sleep?' (same five-point scale; 75.5%, 16.2%, 5.5%, 2.8%). No item means or SDs reported.
primary_models.dv: Sleep disturbance, caregiver-reported 26-item Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children (SDSC), items rated 1 (never) to 5 (daily) and summed; dichotomized as absent (SDSC < 39) vs present (SDSC >= 39) per the scale developers' cutoff. Prevalence of sleep disturbance not reported.

primary_models.equation: logit(P(SleepDisturbance[i] = 1)) = b0 + b1*BedtimeItem[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4..b8*race_ethnicity + b9..b12*sexual_orientation + b13..b17*income + b18*parent_ed + b19..b22*siblings + b23*covid_period + site terms
primary_models.estimation: Stata 18. Multivariable logistic regression per the methods (p. 564); note the table footnote describes the output as coming from 'modified Poisson and linear regression models' while the column is labeled OR. ABCD sample weights based on the American Community Survey applied. Two-sided alpha = .05; no multiple-comparison correction reported. Effect modification by sex, race/ethnicity, sexual orientation, household income, and parent education tested for the bedtime screen use mean score and total screen time; sex interactions additionally tested for each bedtime screen use item (Table 5). Race/ethnicity and sexual orientation interactions reported as non-significant (not shown). It is not explicitly stated whether each bedtime item was entered in a separate model.

primary_models.name: Multivariable linear regression of sleep duration (hours) on bedtime phone/SM behaviors, adjusted for sociodemographics and site, ACS-weighted
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 4, Sleep duration columns (p. 568); methods p. 564; results p. 565; sex-stratified version in Table 5 (see M3)
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional, ABCD Year 3 follow-up; IV and DV measured at the same visit. One observation per participant.
primary_models.sample: Same as M1: N = 10,305, Year 3, mean age 12.93 (SD 0.65), 48.4% female.
primary_models.iv: Same three qualifying bedtime items as M1, each on the five-point Likert scale (1 = never to 5 = every night). No means or SDs reported.
primary_models.dv: Sleep duration in hours from the adolescent-reported Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (MCTQ), using reported bed and wake times on weekdays and weekends; average weekly sleep duration computed as a weighted average of weekday and weekend duration (the paper describes the weights as 'weekdays (7) and weekends (2)'). Higher value = longer sleep. Mean and SD not reported.

covariates.detail: Age, sex, race and ethnicity, sexual orientation, household income, parent education, number of siblings, COVID-19 pandemic period, study site

primary_models.estimation: Stata 18. Multivariable linear regression with ACS-based ABCD sample weights. Two-sided alpha = .05; no multiple-comparison correction. Same interaction testing as M1; sex interactions per item shown in Table 5.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: OR models: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3)/pi (Chinn 2000). B models: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2*beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1) - not computable here because SD_IV and SD_DV are not reported.
d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1-point increase on the five-point bedtime frequency Likert scale (1 = never to 5 = every night) for each item.
d_transformation.notes: ORs (M1, M4) convert via Chinn without additional inputs. For B models (M2, M3), the paper reports no mean or SD for the bedtime Likert items (Table 2 gives only categorical frequencies: 0, 1-2, 3-4, 5-7 nights) and no mean or SD for MCTQ sleep duration, so standardized d cannot be derived from the PDF; online supplement may contain them. Baseline prevalence of SDSC >= 39 is not reported (not needed for Chinn). Methods describe logistic regression for sleep disturbance, but table footnotes mention modified Poisson; columns are labeled OR. [complete-stage check 2026-10-01] Re-read full PDF (pp.562-571): all 12 estimates and CIs present and match Tables 4-5; no SEs/t printed; no SDs for Likert items or sleep duration; SDSC prevalence not printed; no supplement file available in docs/pdfs.

extraction_flags: 1) The methods describe logistic regression for SDSC sleep disturbance, but the table footnotes say the output comes from "modified Poisson and linear regression" models. The columns are labeled OR, so I recorded the values as OR. 2) The paper does not say whether each bedtime item was fit in its own model or whether all items were entered together; "in addition to all variables listed" in the footnote is ambiguous. 3) No SDs are reported for the 1-5 Likert bedtime items or for MCTQ sleep duration, so the B models (M2, M3) cannot be converted to d. The ORs can be converted with the Chinn formula. 4) I included the item about being woken by "phone calls, text messages, or emails" as phone-qualifying even though emails could come from a non-phone device; please check that call. I excluded the night-waking "phone or other device ... play games/browse ..." item as a mixed composite (OR 1.25, B -0.25); coders may want to revisit it. 5) I extracted the sex-stratified Table 5 estimates as separate cards (M3 linear, M4 logistic) because the authors interpret the sex differences. If you prefer, strike them or treat them as interaction results. 6) The ABCD release is not stated, and the online Appendices A and B are not in the PDF. 7) The paper's description of the sleep-duration weights ("weekdays (7) and weekends (2)") is copied as written but looks like an error for 5/2. All 12 values were checked against the Table 4 and Table 5 text.
